commands.short: Let agents publish to this repo with --yes, for a while (needs a person at a console)
commands.long:
agents allow lets coding agents on this machine publish to one repo pair with --yes, without the
console code, for 1h, 6h (the default), 1d, 7d, 15d, 30d or 90d, or --until-revoked. Making the grant itself needs a
person to type a code at a console, so an agent cannot grant itself. Agents still need a green gate
and a clean leak scan for every publish. Grants live on this machine only.

flags.name: for
flags.usage: how long: 1h, 6h (default), 1d, 7d, 15d, 30d or 90d

flags.name: plan
flags.usage: preview the grant without making it

flags.name: until-revoked
flags.usage: never expire; take it back with ghostbranch agents revoke

commands.short: Take back the agent grant for this repo (or --all); needs no console

flags.name: all
flags.usage: revoke every grant in this workspace (also clears a grants.json that isn't valid JSON; a file from a newer Ghostbranch is kept); with --repo, every grant for that repo

flags.name: plan
flags.usage: preview what would be revoked

commands.short: List agent grants, and whether the current token can publish to the public repo
Publish a saved plan if the repos still match it
commands.long: apply publishes a plan saved by promote. It refuses with exit 6 if public main, the feature, the overlay or the gate candidate moved since the plan was made. Re-running it finishes an interrupted publish. A person confirms on the console, or --yes publishes under an agent grant.

flags.name: yes
flags.usage: publish under an agent grant (ghostbranch agents allow); on its own it never skips the console

commands.short: Report what keeps the shadow repo's CI from matching public CI
commands.long:
audit reads the workflows the shadow repo's CI runs and reports repo guards (jobs that skip in
the shadow repo), referenced secrets and which are missing (when the token may list them), workflows a
sync starts in the shadow repo and the guard that stops them, billed Actions minutes, and whether
Ghostbranch's managed overlay files are current. It changes nothing.

commands.short: Show the token's source, account, kind and expiry, and whether it can publish
commands.long:
auth status shows where the token comes from (GHOSTBRANCH_TOKEN, the stored login, GH_TOKEN,
GITHUB_TOKEN or gh), its account and kind, whether it can publish to this checkout's pair (or --repo),
and the stored login. Offline, it still shows the stored login. With GHOSTBRANCH_TOKEN set it doesn't
read the keychain at all. A stored login near expiry is refreshed first, as any command would.

commands.short: Check this machine's setup and the pair, and name each fix; changes nothing
commands.long:
doctor runs six checks, in order: tools (git and this binary), token (its source, account,
expiry, whether it can publish, and the permissions each command group needs), pair (both repos,
the overlay and its config, shadow main, the managed files), guard (the pre-push hook in this
checkout), state (this machine's records) and ci (the audit's summary). Each is ok, warn, fail or
skipped, and names the command that fixes it. It never writes, never prompts and isn't ledgered.
In a checkout of a pair it checks that pair; --repo names another; with neither it skips the
checks that need a pair. It exits 0 unless a check fails (DOCTOR_FAILED, details.failed).

commands.short: Explain an error, warning or exit code, and what to do about it
commands.long: explain prints what a code means, its usual causes, what to do, and whether a person must act. It needs no token and no network. --all lists every code.

flags.name: all
flags.usage: list every exit, error and warning code

commands.short: Park a feature: keep its branch, but leave it out of feature list
commands.long:
feature abandon marks a feature abandoned in its metadata in the shadow repo. Nothing is deleted:
its branch, gate and plans stay, status still shows it, and feature list hides it unless --all.
--undo makes it an active feature again. To delete a feature, use feature close.

flags.name: plan
flags.usage: preview exactly what would change, and change nothing (same as --dry-run)

flags.name: undo
flags.usage: restore an abandoned feature

commands.short: Delete a feature from the shadow repo (a person confirms unless it merged unchanged)
commands.long:
feature close deletes a feature from the shadow repo: its branch, its gate branch, its metadata
and its plan refs, in one push that fails, deleting nothing, if any of them moved since it looked. Then it
closes the gate's draft PR and removes the feature's plan files and mirror refs on this machine. The
ledger records every ref deleted with the SHA it pointed at, so a branch can be pushed back.

A feature whose public PR merged and whose branch hasn't moved since closes without asking (sync does
this on its own). Anything else would lose work that was never published, so a person confirms by
typing a code at the console. --plan shows what would be deleted and asks no one.

flags.name: plan
flags.usage: preview exactly what would change, and change nothing (same as --dry-run)

commands.short: Fold a stacked feature into its parent: the parent fast-forwards to it, and it closes
commands.long:
feature fold moves the parent feature's branch to <feature>'s head in the shadow repo, a fast-forward
(never a merge or a rebase), and closes <feature>. Its branch, gate branch, metadata and plan refs are deleted
in the same atomic push, leased on what fold read, and the features stacked on <feature> are stacked on the
parent instead. Nothing is lost: every commit of <feature> is on the parent, so no console is asked.
If the parent has moved on since <feature> was started from it, fold refuses with FOLD_NEEDS_REBASE, and next
gives the git commands to rebase <feature> yourself. Ghostbranch never resolves conflicts. --plan shows what
would change.

flags.name: plan
flags.usage: preview exactly what would change, and change nothing (same as --dry-run)

commands.short: List the pair's features with their state, drift, gate and public PR
commands.long:
feature list prints one line per feature: its state, whether it still merges cleanly onto public
main (drift), its last gate and its public PR. Abandoned features are left out unless --all. It only reads.

flags.name: all
flags.usage: include abandoned features

commands.short: Bring commits someone made on a feature's open public PR into its shadow branch
commands.long:
feature pull reads the open public PR of <feature> and the commits on its branch that Ghostbranch didn't
publish (someone pushed them on GitHub: a maintainer's fix, an applied suggestion). It brings them into the
feature's branch in the shadow repo and records them as adopted, in one push leased on what it read. They
are already public, so the next gate doesn't scan them again; the next promote keeps them. Your later commits
are replayed on top of them. A merge commit or a conflict stops it with the git steps to merge the PR's branch
yourself; Ghostbranch never resolves conflicts. It only touches the shadow repo; your checkout needs a fetch
and reset afterwards. --plan shows what would change.

flags.name: plan
flags.usage: preview exactly what would change, and change nothing (same as --dry-run)

commands.short: Rebase the features stacked above <feature> onto its tip, in the shadow repo
commands.long:
feature restack replays each feature stacked above <feature> (then the ones above those, in order)
onto its parent's new tip, in a throwaway worktree, and pushes each with a lease, together with its updated
record. A feature that already holds its parent's tip only has its record updated. The first conflict stops
the restack with the git commands to rebase that feature yourself; features already restacked stay
restacked. Ghostbranch never resolves conflicts.
With --onto main or --onto <feature>, <feature> itself moves first: its own commits are replayed onto main
(dropping its parent's commits) or onto that feature, and then the features above it follow.
It only touches the shadow repo; your checkouts of the rewritten branches need a fetch and reset afterwards.

flags.name: onto
flags.usage: move <feature> itself onto "main" or onto another feature first

flags.name: plan
flags.usage: preview exactly what would change, and change nothing (same as --dry-run)

commands.short: Show one feature in full: state, drift, gate, PR, commits and ledger
commands.long:
feature show prints everything about one feature: its state, branch and base, drift onto public
main and the files that conflict, its last gate, its public PR and plan, its commits since public main,
and this pair's ledger entries for it. It only reads.

commands.short: Start a feature branch in the shadow repo
commands.long: feature start creates <name> from shadow main in the shadow repo and records it as a feature. It does not touch your checkout; fetch and switch to the branch afterwards. With --from <feature> it starts at that feature's tip instead and records it as the parent, stacking the new feature on it.

flags.name: from
flags.usage: stack the feature on another feature: start it at that feature's tip in the shadow repo (default: shadow main)

flags.name: plan
flags.usage: preview exactly what would change, and change nothing (same as --dry-run)

flags.name: yes
flags.usage: accepted for consistency; feature start never asks

commands.short: Rebase on public main, scan for leaks, and run CI; report only
commands.long:
gate rebases the feature onto public main, scans exactly what would be published for leaks,
pushes a CI candidate (the feature plus the overlay) to a draft PR in the shadow repo, and waits for
every check. It records the result and never touches the public repo. Exit 3 means the gate failed.
With --detach it returns a job id once CI has started; ghostbranch wait <job> finishes it, from this machine or another. Without --detach, Ctrl-C leaves the job pending for wait.

flags.name: detach
flags.usage: push the candidate, record the job and return without waiting for CI; finish it with ghostbranch wait <job>

flags.name: plan
flags.usage: preview exactly what would change, and change nothing (same as --dry-run)

commands.short: Check a push to the public repo; run by the pre-push hook with git's input on stdin
Install the pre-push guard in this checkout

flags.name: plan
flags.usage: show what would change, and change nothing

commands.short: Show whether the guard is installed here, and what it covers
Remove the pre-push guard, restoring any hook it chained

flags.name: plan
flags.usage: show what would change, and change nothing

commands.short: Print the guide for coding agents, or install a skill that points agents at it
commands.long:
guide prints how coding agents should use Ghostbranch: the loop, the rules, and every exit and
error code. It always matches this binary. --install claude|codex writes a small user-level skill
(never a file in your repo) that tells the agent to read this guide; --uninstall removes it.

flags.name: install
flags.usage: write a user-level skill for an agent: claude or codex

flags.name: plan
flags.usage: show what would be written, and write nothing

flags.name: uninstall
flags.usage: remove the skill for an agent: claude or codex

commands.short: Create or adopt the private shadow repo for a public repo
commands.long:
init creates <owner/repo>-shadow as a private repo (or adopts an existing one with --adopt),
mirrors the public repo's branches and tags into it, and creates the "ghostbranch" overlay branch,
which holds .ghostbranch.yml and is the shadow repo's default branch. It never writes to the public
repo. Running it again resumes a partial setup.
Run by a person at a terminal with an answer missing, it asks: the public repo (from origin), a
login if there is none, the shadow repo, the push guard (in a clone of the public repo) and
scheduled sync. It shows the --plan preview, then runs init, guard install and doctor, and ends
with how to start a first feature. Flags answer the questions; --json, --non-interactive and --yes
never ask.

flags.name: adopt
flags.usage: take over an existing, empty or mirror-only, private repo

flags.name: guard
flags.usage: install the push guard in this checkout, a clone of the public repo, after init

flags.name: no-guard
flags.usage: don't install the push guard, and don't ask

flags.name: no-sync
flags.usage: leave scheduled sync off, and don't ask

flags.name: plan
flags.usage: preview exactly what would change, and change nothing (same as --dry-run)

flags.name: shadow
flags.usage: shadow repo name (default <owner/repo>-shadow)

flags.name: sync
flags.usage: turn on scheduled sync in the new overlay (sync.schedule "23 */6 * * *", about 120 Actions minutes a month)

flags.name: yes
flags.usage: never ask: use the flags given and the defaults

commands.short: Show the ledger of what ghostbranch did on this machine, newest first
commands.long:
log prints this workspace's ledger: every mutating command, who ran it (the actor), and how it
ended, newest first. It reads only the local ledger: no token, no network, no pair. --feature and --op
match exactly, --actor matches a prefix (agent: shows every agent), and --since takes a duration back
from now (24h) or an RFC 3339 time. --repo shows one pair's entries, even after remove; --repo . is the
pair this checkout's remotes name.

flags.name: actor
flags.usage: only entries whose actor starts with this, such as agent: or human:octo

flags.name: feature
flags.usage: only entries about this feature

flags.name: limit
flags.usage: at most this many entries (1 or more)

flags.name: op
flags.usage: only entries for this operation, such as promote or "feature start"

flags.name: since
flags.usage: only entries from this long ago (24h) or since this RFC 3339 time

commands.short: Log in to GitHub with the Ghostbranch GitHub App, or store a token from stdin
commands.long:
login runs GitHub's device flow for the Ghostbranch GitHub App: it shows a code and a URL on the
console, opens the browser when it can, and waits while you approve. The token reaches only the repos
you install the app on, refreshes itself, and is kept in the OS keychain (never in a file).
With --with-token it reads one token from stdin instead (never from an argument, so it stays out of
shell history), checks it with GitHub, and stores it. GHOSTBRANCH_TOKEN, when set, still wins over
the stored login.

flags.name: with-token
flags.usage: read a token from stdin and store it

commands.short: Remove the stored GitHub login from the OS keychain
commands.long:
logout removes the login that ghostbranch login stored in the OS keychain, a corrupt one included.
It can't revoke the token at GitHub (that needs the app's client secret, which Ghostbranch doesn't
ship); for a GitHub App login it gives the page where you revoke the app's access. Environment tokens
(GHOSTBRANCH_TOKEN, GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN) are untouched.

commands.short: Publish a gated feature, or a stack of them, to the public repo as PRs
commands.long:
promote reuses a fresh green gate (or runs one), builds the public commits (each feature commit
with --mode preserve, one with squash, or the groups of a --curate file) on public main, ending on
exactly the gated tree, scans every commit's files, message and author, the branch name and PR text
for leaks, and saves a plan.
With --plan it stops there. Otherwise a person confirms by typing a code shown on the console, or, if they have allowed agents with "ghostbranch agents allow", --yes publishes. Without either it stops at the plan with exit 5.
Several features, bottom first (promote a b c), publish a stack: each branch's PR is based on the
branch below (a's on main) and shows only that branch's commits, and one approval covers every PR.
Each branch needs a fresh green gate built on the branch below. Where GitHub offers native stacked
PRs, they are registered as one stack. --mode-for and --title-for set one branch's mode and PR title.

flags.name: body
flags.usage: PR body (default: the commit's body, or one line per commit)

flags.name: branch
flags.usage: public branch name (default: the feature name)

flags.name: curate
flags.usage: curated mode: a JSON file {"commits": [{"from": [<sha>...], "message": "..."}]} naming every feature commit once, in the order to publish

flags.name: detach
flags.usage: if a gate is needed, start it and return its job instead of waiting

flags.name: message
flags.usage: the squash commit's message (squash mode only)

flags.name: mode
flags.usage: history mode: preserve (each commit), squash (one commit) or curated (a --curate file); default promote.default_mode, which is preserve unless set

flags.name: mode-for
flags.usage: one branch's history mode in a stack promote: <feature>=squash or <feature>=preserve (repeatable); default --mode

flags.name: plan
flags.usage: save and print the plan without publishing

flags.name: title
flags.usage: PR title (needed when more than one commit is published; default: the only commit's subject, or the squash message's first line)

flags.name: title-for
flags.usage: one branch's PR title in a stack promote: <feature>=<title> (repeatable)

flags.name: yes
flags.usage: publish under an agent grant (ghostbranch agents allow); on its own it never skips the console

commands.short: Unregister the pair from this machine (needs a person at a console)
commands.long:
remove takes the pair off this machine: it revokes the pair's agent grants and waivers, deletes
its plan files and its local mirror, and drops it from the workspace. Nothing on GitHub changes: the
shadow repo, its branches and features stay, and the ledger keeps its history. Because it drops grants
and waivers, a person confirms by typing a code at the console; --plan shows what would go. It needs
no GitHub token.

flags.name: plan
flags.usage: preview exactly what would change, and change nothing (same as --dry-run)

commands.short: Pair health and every feature's state
commands.long:
status reports whether shadow main is behind public main, whether the overlay's managed files
need an upgrade, and whether scheduled sync is on; then every feature, abandoned ones included, with its
state, whether it still merges cleanly onto public main (drift), its last gate and its public PR. It only
reads: nothing is pushed and nothing is written to the ledger.

commands.short: Fast-forward shadow main to public main
commands.long:
sync fast-forwards the shadow repo's main to public main. It never force-pushes: if shadow main has diverged it stops with exit 4.
Its pushes start the shadow repo's push-triggered workflows, which re-test what public CI already tested,
so it then cancels those runs (the token needs Actions write on the shadow repo); --no-cancel leaves them running.
Last, it closes each feature whose public PR merged and whose branch hasn't moved since it was published,
as feature close does; --no-close leaves them. It never closes a feature that needs a person.

flags.name: no-cancel
flags.usage: don't cancel the workflow runs the sync's pushes start in the shadow repo

flags.name: no-close
flags.usage: don't close features whose public PR merged

flags.name: plan
flags.usage: preview exactly what would change, and change nothing (same as --dry-run)

flags.name: yes
flags.usage: accepted for consistency; sync never asks

commands.short: Bring the pair's Ghostbranch-managed overlay files up to date
commands.long:
upgrade compares the overlay branch's managed files (today the opt-in sync workflow) with this
version's templates and .ghostbranch.yml, then adds, updates or removes them in one overlay commit.
Turning scheduled sync on or off is: edit sync.schedule, then run upgrade. A file someone edited by hand
is replaced; --plan shows that first. It writes only the shadow repo's overlay branch, then runs the audit.

flags.name: plan
flags.usage: preview exactly what would change, and change nothing (same as --dry-run)

flags.name: yes
flags.usage: accepted for consistency; upgrade never asks

commands.short: Print this binary's version
commands.long: version prints this binary's module version and VCS commit, and the JSON contract version it speaks. ghostbranch --version does the same.

commands.short: Wait for a gate job's CI and record its result
commands.long: wait finishes a gate started with --detach (or interrupted): it waits for the candidate's CI, records the result, and prints what gate would have. A finished job answers at once. With --json it streams one JSON event per line on stdout, and the last line is the result envelope.

flags.name: timeout
flags.usage: stop waiting after this long and report pending; the job keeps running (0, the default, waits until CI settles)

commands.short: Waive leak findings that are false positives (needs a person at a console)
commands.long:
waivers add lets a publish go ahead despite leak findings a person has checked and judged safe,
such as a fake key in a test fixture. It rebases, strips and scans the feature again on this machine
(no push, no CI), shows each finding at the console, and needs a person to type a code: an agent
cannot waive. A waiver covers exactly that content in that file; changed content is a new finding.
Findings in the commit message, branch or PR text are never waivable: change the text instead.
Waivers live on this machine only.

flags.name: plan
flags.usage: show what would be waived without waiving it

flags.name: reason
flags.usage: why these findings are safe to publish (recorded in the ledger)

commands.short: List waivers for this repo (or every repo when none can be told apart)
Revoke waivers for this repo, or every waiver with --all; needs no console

flags.name: all
flags.usage: revoke every waiver in this workspace (also clears a waivers.json that isn't valid JSON; a file from a newer Ghostbranch is kept)

flags.name: plan
flags.usage: preview what would be revoked

global_flags.name: dry-run
global_flags.usage: preview exactly what would change, and change nothing

global_flags.name: json
global_flags.usage: print JSON on stdout: one object (wait streams one event per line, the result last)

global_flags.name: no-color
global_flags.usage: never colour human output (NO_COLOR does the same)

global_flags.name: non-interactive
global_flags.usage: never prompt; missing input is an error

global_flags.name: repo
global_flags.usage: public or shadow repo (owner/name) to act on
